title: Engineering Enablement Programs
framing: How I build enablement programs, worked example: MuleSoft Days, a training program I designed and iterated through three in-person pilots before turning it into a 12-module self-paced course — 53+ documented participants, with continued organic use years after I handed it off. The office-hours/coaching cadence below is a proposed extension, not something the original program had.

case_study.name: MuleSoft Days
case_study.problem: Mutual of Omaha launched a major initiative to move to API-led architecture, choosing MuleSoft as the platform. I was on the team that brought MuleSoft into the company and became a subject matter expert on it. As teams started onboarding, a real training gap surfaced fast: the official MuleSoft and third-party training only covered how MuleSoft worked out of the box, not our highly customized instance — a custom CI/CD pipeline, plus the added complexity of running both CloudHub (cloud runtimes) and Runtime Fabric (on-prem runtimes) side by side. Without coherent training, the initiative's timeline was genuinely at risk.
case_study.approach: I built the program iteratively rather than designing it top-down: a two-week in-person pilot with six participants, refined to one week for the second run, then refined again to five half-day in-person sessions plus self-paced work for the third. Taking what each round taught me, I turned it into a 12-module, self-paced, hands-on course carrying a novice MuleSoft developer to intermediate proficiency, anchored throughout in the company's actual golden-path pattern rather than generic MuleSoft concepts.
case_study.outcome: 53+ documented participants, with consistently positive feedback and survey results. I refreshed the videos about a year after the initial release; the program has run largely unmaintained since I moved to other initiatives, and it shows in places — the CI/CD module still references Bitbucket and Jenkins, since replaced by GitHub — but the core content on MuleSoft development, testing, and the company's architecture has stayed relevant enough that new MuleSoft engineers still use it today.

learning_path.title: Specification Driven Development
learning_path.description: Writing and agreeing on the API specification before implementation begins, rather than letting the contract emerge from the code.

learning_path.title: CTPSP MuleSoft API Template
learning_path.description: The company's golden-path starting point for a new MuleSoft API, onboarded to the Common Technology Platform Service Portal.

learning_path.title: CI/CD Pipeline (Bitbucket & Jenkins)
learning_path.description: Building and deploying through the company's actual pipeline tooling, not a generic MuleSoft CI/CD walkthrough. (Now the one part of the course that's genuinely dated — the company has since moved to GitHub.)

learning_path.title: MuleSoft Flow Development
learning_path.description: Core flow-building fundamentals in Anypoint Studio.

learning_path.title: Implementing MUnit Tests
learning_path.description: Automated testing for MuleSoft flows using MuleSoft's own MUnit framework.

learning_path.title: Refactoring and Further Development of an Existing API
learning_path.description: Working inside an API that already exists and has real constraints, not just building greenfield.

learning_path.title: API Alerts and Functional Monitoring
learning_path.description: Setting up monitoring and alerting for an API once it's deployed, not just building it and walking away.

learning_path.title: EDP & CTP Support Services
learning_path.description: Who to go to for what: the Enterprise Developer Platform (EDP) team that owns MuleSoft, and the broader Common Technology Platform (CTP) Agile Release Train it belongs to, alongside other platform capabilities like CTPSP.

learning_path.title: Understanding MuleSoft Architecture at Mutual of Omaha
learning_path.description: The company's specific MuleSoft architecture, including the dual-runtime model (CloudHub and Runtime Fabric) that made a generic MuleSoft course insufficient in the first place.

cadence.title: Weekly office hours
cadence.description: A standing, low-friction slot for whoever's mid-module and stuck — optional, drop-in, no prep required on either side.

cadence.title: Cohort check-ins
cadence.description: A lightweight touchpoint partway through a cohort's progression, surfacing where the curriculum itself is unclear before it becomes everyone's individual problem.

cadence.title: Escalation to 1:1 coaching
cadence.description: For anyone still stuck after office hours — the exception path, not the default, so the self-paced model stays the primary on-ramp rather than becoming shadow 1:1 training.

reinforcement: 53+ documented participants and consistently positive survey feedback validated the format well before organic reuse did.
Still in active use by new MuleSoft engineers today, years after the last real update — the clearest evidence a program actually stuck rather than fading once the launch push ended.

Honest about its own decay: the CI/CD module still teaches Bitbucket and Jenkins, since replaced by GitHub. The rest of the content — MuleSoft development, testing, the company's actual architecture — has aged far better than the tooling around it.
